items.stimulus:
The two-day weekend feels so natural today that it is easy to assume it has always existed. In fact, for most of history the working week had no fixed shape. Farm work followed the seasons and the weather rather than the calendar, and the main regular pause was a religious day of rest.

Industrialisation changed this. Factories needed machines to run continuously and workers to arrive at the same hour, so employers pressed for long, regular weeks, often six days of twelve hours or more. Workers did not simply accept this. In parts of nineteenth-century Britain, many skilled craftsmen observed what was called 'Saint Monday': after being paid on Saturday and resting on Sunday, they stayed away from work on Monday too, making up the lost hours later in the week. Employers complained, but because many craftsmen were paid by the piece rather than by the hour, they found the custom hard to stamp out.

Over time, a compromise emerged. Employers offered a shorter Saturday, with work finishing in the early afternoon, in exchange for reliable attendance on Monday. Reformers supported the change, arguing that a free Saturday afternoon could be spent on improving activities such as education or sport, rather than on the drinking associated with Saint Monday. Organised leisure grew around the new free time: football matches, for example, were increasingly scheduled for Saturday afternoons.

The full two-day weekend arrived later and unevenly. In the early twentieth century some manufacturers in the United States experimented with a five-day week, and by the middle of the century it had become standard in many industrialised countries, helped by laws limiting weekly hours. Its spread was not driven by generosity alone. Some employers argued that rested workers made fewer errors, and that people with free time would spend more money on goods and leisure.

This history suggests that the weekend was neither a gift handed down from above nor simply a victory won from below. It was a negotiated settlement, shaped by workers' habits, employers' need for predictability and changing ideas about how free time should be used.

items.stimulus:
A museum curator, Ilona Varga, meets Edmund Rask, whose grandfather donated the painting 'The Harvest Feast' by the nineteenth-century artist Corvin Haldane (both the painting and the artist are fictional).

Rask: My grandfather gave this museum 'The Harvest Feast' on the understanding that it would be shown. It has been in storage for six years. That is not what he intended.

Varga: I understand. The painting is technically superb, but its servants are drawn as crude caricatures that many visitors find hurtful. We have been planning how to show it responsibly.

Rask: 'Responsibly' usually means surrounding it with panels that tell people what to think. Haldane was a painter of his time. Judge the brushwork, not the politics.

Varga: The brushwork and the politics are on the same canvas. If we hang it without context, visitors may assume the museum shares its attitudes. A panel doesn't tell people what to think; it tells them what they are looking at.

Rask: Then why not let visitors decide for themselves whether to be offended? Adults can cope with an old picture.

Varga: Some will cope. Others will leave and never come back. A public museum has to serve everyone, including the communities the painting mocks. Our proposal is to hang it in a new room alongside work by artists from those communities, responding to it.

Rask: So my grandfather's gift becomes the villain of someone else's exhibition.

Varga: Not a villain, a starting point. Hidden in storage, it helps no one. Displayed with care, it could become the most discussed work in the building.

Rask: I suppose being discussed is better than being forgotten. But I want the label to describe Haldane's skill as well as his faults.

Varga: That's a fair request, and I think our writers will agree.

For eleven days the square kept no time.

No one looked at him. That was as it should be.
The best repairs, he told his apprentice later,
are the ones the town forgets were ever needed.

items.stimulus:
Imagine you were asked to design the rules of a society, deciding how wealth, opportunities and duties are shared, but with one unusual condition: you would not know what position you yourself would occupy in that society. You might be born rich or poor, healthy or ill, talented or ordinary. This thought experiment, made famous by the twentieth-century philosopher John Rawls, is known as choosing behind a 'veil of ignorance'.

The point of the veil is to remove bias. People who know they are wealthy tend to favour low taxes; people who know they are poor tend to favour generous public services. Behind the veil, no one can tailor the rules to their own advantage, so, the argument goes, whatever rules they would agree on can be considered fair.

Rawls believed that rational people in this situation would be cautious. Because they might end up among the worst off, they would want to make the worst position as good as possible. They would therefore accept inequalities only if those inequalities improved the situation of the least advantaged. For instance, higher pay for surgeons might be acceptable if it led more people to train as surgeons and so improved care for everyone, including the poor.

Critics have challenged this conclusion. Some argue that people behind the veil might be willing to gamble: a society with a small chance of hardship but a large chance of great wealth could seem attractive to someone who enjoys risk. Others say the experiment strips away too much. A person who does not know their talents, values or commitments, they claim, is hardly a person at all, so it is unclear why such a person's imagined choices should bind real people.

Even so, the veil remains a useful test. When we are tempted to defend a rule, we can ask whether we would still accept it if we did not know which side of it we would end up on.

Some argue that people behind the veil might be willing to gamble: a society with a small chance of hardship but a large chance of great wealth could seem attractive to someone who enjoys risk. Others say the experiment strips away too much. A person who does not know their talents, values or commitments, they claim, is hardly a person at all, so it is unclear why such a person's imagined choices should bind real people.

Even so, the veil remains a useful test. When we are tempted to defend a rule, we can ask whether we would still accept it if we did not know which side of it we would end up on.

items.stimulus:
Imagine you were asked to design the rules of a society, deciding how wealth, opportunities and duties are shared, but with one unusual condition: you would not know what position you yourself would occupy in that society. You might be born rich or poor, healthy or ill, talented or ordinary. This thought experiment, made famous by the twentieth-century philosopher John Rawls, is known as choosing behind a 'veil of ignorance'.

The point of the veil is to remove bias. People who know they are wealthy tend to favour low taxes; people who know they are poor tend to favour generous public services. Behind the veil, no one can tailor the rules to their own advantage, so, the argument goes, whatever rules they would agree on can be considered fair.

Rawls believed that rational people in this situation would be cautious. Because they might end up among the worst off, they would want to make the worst position as good as possible. They would therefore accept inequalities only if those inequalities improved the situation of the least advantaged. For instance, higher pay for surgeons might be acceptable if it led more people to train as surgeons and so improved care for everyone, including the poor.

Critics have challenged this conclusion. Some argue that people behind the veil might be willing to gamble: a society with a small chance of hardship but a large chance of great wealth could seem attractive to someone who enjoys risk. Others say the experiment strips away too much. A person who does not know their talents, values or commitments, they claim, is hardly a person at all, so it is unclear why such a person's imagined choices should bind real people.

Even so, the veil remains a useful test. When we are tempted to defend a rule, we can ask whether we would still accept it if we did not know which side of it we would end up on.

items.stimulus:
Every election season, the same ritual unfolds. A famous singer posts a photograph with a candidate, an actor records a video urging fans to vote, and a sports star appears on stage at a rally. Campaign managers love these endorsements because they attract attention cheaply. I think voters should treat them with suspicion, and candidates should rely on them far less.

The first problem is that fame in one field does not bring expertise in another. A footballer may know a great deal about football, but nothing about his fame makes him a better judge of tax policy or hospital funding than the voter scrolling past his post. When we are persuaded by a celebrity, we are borrowing the confidence of someone who has not necessarily done any more thinking than we have.

The second problem is that endorsements replace argument with emotion. A candidate who can stand beside a beloved performer does not need to explain how a policy will work; the warm feelings fans have for the star are simply transferred to the politician. Over time, this rewards campaigns that are good at collecting famous friends rather than campaigns with good ideas.

Defenders of endorsements say that celebrities draw young people into politics who would otherwise ignore it. Yet the evidence for this is weaker than it appears. In the last national election in my country, the candidate with the most celebrity endorsements lost, so clearly endorsements do not change how people vote, and they cannot be credited with engaging anyone.

None of this means that famous people should stay silent. They are citizens like the rest of us and are entitled to their opinions. But a citizen's vote should be guided by what candidates propose and how they have behaved, not by who has been photographed with them. If campaigns spent the money and energy they now devote to celebrity appearances on explaining their policies, our elections would be better informed and our choices more truly our own.

items.stimulus:
Long before writing, communities preserved histories, laws and family lines in stories that might take hours to perform. How could a storyteller hold so much in memory? Researchers who have studied living oral traditions point to several techniques.

One is the formula: a ready-made phrase that fits the rhythm of a line and can be reused whenever it is needed. In a tradition of this kind, a hero might always be 'quick-handed' and a river always 'grey-backed'. Such phrases are not lazy repetition. They give the performer a stock of building blocks, so that attention can go to the shape of the story rather than to finding words.

A second technique links a story to places. In some traditions, each episode is tied to a feature of the landscape, such as a rock, a river bend or a hill, so that travelling through the land, or imagining doing so, calls up the next part of the narrative. The landscape becomes a kind of index.

Third, many oral performances rely on music, rhythm and gesture. A melody limits which words can fit, and a performer who forgets a line may recover it by recalling the tune or the movement that goes with it.

Interestingly, fieldworkers have found that performers who claim to tell a story 'exactly as I learned it' often vary the wording considerably from one performance to the next, while keeping the sequence of events and the key names stable. What is preserved, it seems, is less the precise words than the structure and the essential facts, which is exactly what these techniques are best suited to protect.

Few forms of entertainment have changed as much in recent decades as the circus. Acts featuring lions, elephants and bears were once the main attraction; today many countries restrict or ban the use of wild animals in travelling shows. Supporters of these bans and their critics disagree not only about facts but also about which moral questions matter most.

The case against animal acts usually begins with welfare. Travelling circuses move frequently, and animals may spend long periods in transport cages and temporary enclosures far smaller than their natural ranges. Training, critics add, has often relied on punishment. Even where there is no cruelty, they argue, an animal whose life is organised around performing tricks for crowds cannot express much of its natural behaviour.

Defenders reply that these problems are not unavoidable. Some modern circuses say they use only reward-based training and provide spacious, enriched enclosures. Domestic animals such as horses and dogs, they point out, have performed alongside humans for centuries and may even benefit from the exercise and attention involved. If welfare is the concern, they argue, the right response is strict regulation and inspection rather than an outright ban.

A deeper objection is not about suffering at all. Some philosophers argue that using animals purely as a spectacle treats them as objects for human amusement, and that this is wrong even if the animals are well cared for. On this view, the question is not whether a performing elephant is content but whether we have any right to make it perform.

These positions lead to different policies. Those who focus on welfare may support a licensing system that permits some animal acts under strict conditions. Those who object to the use itself are likely to oppose any animal performance, however humane. Before debating particular laws, then, we should be clear about which of these concerns we are trying to address, because a rule that satisfies one may do nothing to answer the other.
